column4: Livestock carry burdens to a land, بَلَدٍ, that people could reach only with severe personal hardship; this directly stages the load-bearing mount, the road, and exhaustion together.
The Trust, ٱلْأَمَانَةَ, is offered as something to be carried; creation refuses it and the human carries it, joining reliability to the danger of accepting a load beyond one's faithfulness.
Unbelievers promise travelers on their path, ٱتَّبِعُوا۟ سَبِيلَنَا, that they will carry their sins, yet carry none and are called liars; load, road, and كذب meet in one ayah.
They will carry their own burdens and further burdens with them; this supplies the actual load that the false promise in 29:12 denied.

Those charged to carry the Torah but failing to carry it are likened to a donkey carrying books, a precise moral version of a beast that bears a load without completing the human work entrusted to it.
A heavily laden soul may call another to its load, حِمْلِهَا, but none of it will be carried, setting the limit of even the willing burden-bearer at judgment.
The reward is a camel-load, حِمْلُ بَعِيرٍ, and the speaker guarantees it, joining the section's load camel to personal reliability.
When summoned to go forth, people become heavy and sink to the ground, ٱثَّاقَلْتُمْ إِلَى ٱلْأَرْضِ, an exact human enactment of the mount that rises only to remain stuck.
The command to go forth light or heavy and strive makes willingness, rather than an ideal condition, the answer to remaining behind under one's load.
A near gain and moderate journey would attract them, but the hard distance exposes their false oath; campaigning, road fatigue, and the كذب side of failed endurance coincide.
Had they intended to set out they would have prepared equipment, but they are held back and told to sit; this identifies the practical failure behind the liars of 9:42.
The section itself invokes this ayah: humanity is created in كَبَدٍ, toil, making arduousness the condition of the human road rather than an accidental breakdown.
The section explicitly identifies the human as one who toils toward the Lord and will meet Him, giving the tiring journey its direction and endpoint.
عَامِلَةٌ نَّاصِبَةٌ, laboring and exhausted, fuses work with depletion exactly as the section's work-bred animal can end as a spent one.
Fighters with prophets neither lose heart, weaken, nor yield under what strikes them; their sustained courage is the direct opposite of the charge that starts and then fails.
At Uhud the believers fulfill the attack until they falter, dispute, and disobey; it is a Quranic battle instance of an initially true charge that slackens before completion.
The believers are told not to weaken in pursuing the enemy: both sides feel pain, but only they hope for what is with God, making promised outcome the strength that keeps the pursuit moving.
When meeting a force, believers are commanded to stand firm and remember God; this is the battlefield endurance named by the section's warrior who does not leave his opponent.
Dispute would make them lose courage and their strength depart, so patience preserves the firmness commanded in 8:45.
Believing men prove true to their covenant; some complete their vow and others wait without changing, the human counterpart of a reliable bearer and a charge that does not turn false.
Belief and good work receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ, the exact promise of an uncut reward around which the image sets exhaustion.
After the toiling journey of 84:6, believers who do good works receive أَجْرٌ غَيْرُ مَمْنُونٍ; the destination answers the road's fatigue with reward that does not fail.
The Prophet is promised أَجْرًا غَيْرَ مَمْنُونٍ, directly opposing depletion in sustained prophetic work.
The great character in this ayah stands beside the uncut reward of 68:3, matching the source dictionary's description of the enduring human load-bearer as also good in character.
God charges no soul beyond its capacity, and the prayer asks not to be made to carry an unbearable burden; the ayah defines the merciful limit of load and endurance.
God removes the Prophet's burden, وِزْرَكَ, presenting divine relief as the lifting of an actual load.
The burden named in 94:2 had weighed down his back, the bodily effect expected from an exhausting load.
The best person to hire is ٱلْقَوِىُّ ٱلْأَمِينُ, strong and trustworthy; power to do the work and reliability in doing it remain joined rather than splitting into strength and later failure.
The ifrit offers to carry the throne before Solomon rises and describes himself as strong and trustworthy, لَقَوِىٌّ أَمِينٌ, combining a great load with the qualities of the reliable mount.
True piety gives wealth to the stranded traveler, keeps covenants, and remains patient in hardship and battle; generosity, road need, truthfulness, and endurance converge here.
Giving and guarding oneself begin the path opposite the source dictionary's person who weakens even in generosity.
Confirming the best promise gives truthful continuation to the giver of 92:5.
God eases that giver toward ease, so sustained truth and giving become a passable road.
The counterfigure is stingy and imagines himself self-sufficient, precisely the human weakening in generosity developed under the ب ل د branch.
He denies the best promise, joining withholding to كذب rather than letting denial remain merely verbal.
God eases the denier toward hardship, completing the passage's two opposed roads of ease and difficulty.
The wording ٱلَّذِى يُكَذِّبُ بِٱلدِّينِ directly answers 95:7's question about denial of the Judgment and opens a sequence in which denial appears as failed action.
The denier of Judgment does not urge feeding the poor, making the source dictionary's weakening in generosity a visible consequence of denial.
The same people are heedless of their prayer, a religious work performed without reliable attentiveness.
They withhold even small assistance, completing the practical failure introduced by denial in 107:1.
Paradise contains rivers of milk whose taste never changes, لَبَنٍ لَّمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ طَعْمُهُ; this enduring milk reverses the dictionary scene in which expected camel milk stops too soon.
What people possess runs out while what is with God remains, and the patient are paid for their work; it states the image's passing strength and unspent reward in one contrast.
The people of the Garden receive عَطَاءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, a gift not cut off, directly paraphrasing the section's unbroken wage.
The Garden's food and shade are دائم, enduring, giving concrete provision to the promise that reward does not run dry.
God's provision has no depletion, مَا لَهُۥ مِن نَّفَادٍ, the lasting supply opposite milk, force, or pay that runs out.
The abundant fruit named in 56:32 is neither cut off nor withheld in this ayah, a material image of uninterrupted recompense.
God charges a person only with what He has given and promises ease after hardship, setting capacity and relief around every imposed load.
Human life moves from weakness to strength and then back to weakness and gray age, staging the full arc from the dependable bearer to exhaustion.
Some people are returned, يُرَدُّ, to the most abject age after knowledge, joining the section's root of return to loss of human capacity.
A person may be returned to the most abject age and lose former knowledge, another direct Quranic form of strength ending in incapacity.
Long life brings a reversal in creation, نُنَكِّسْهُ فِى ٱلْخَلْقِ, echoing the section's dictionary gloss of regressing in work and the surah's return downward.
Good work is paired with the rule that no soul is charged beyond its capacity, and its bearers inherit the Garden; measured burden leads to lasting reward.
No soul is charged beyond its capacity, and the truthful record prevents injustice; ability to bear and just judgment are placed together.
Whoever turns away from the Reminder carries a burden on the Day of Resurrection, making failed response into a lasting load.
The carriers remain under that burden, and it is an evil load for them on the Day of Resurrection; this identifies the exhausting consequence of 20:100.
Misleaders carry their own burdens in full and part of the burdens of those they mislead, a load multiplied by failed guidance.
No burdened soul bears another's burden, and all return to the Lord for disclosure; the ayah fixes responsibility at the journey's judicial end.
Guidance or error belongs to its actor, and no bearer carries another's burden; the road chosen cannot be completed by transferring its load.
No bearer bears another's burden before the return to God, while gratitude pleases Him; each traveler remains answerable for the load of response.
No laden soul bears the burden of another, introducing the neighboring rule that each human has only the striving he performs.
The Messenger is responsible for what he is made to carry and the addressees for what they are made to carry, distributing duty as distinct loads.
Those who spend without following the gift with مَنّ, reproach, retain their reward; this other sense of the م ن ن root shows how generosity remains unspoiled.
Believers are told not to nullify charity by reproach and injury; the other Quranic sense of مَنّ names an act that makes a seemingly good work fail.
Two groups are on the verge of losing heart in battle, but God is their protecting ally; the ayah catches the charge at the point where it may slacken.
The command not to weaken or grieve while having the upper hand turns spiritual confidence into the strength to remain in the field.
When meeting an advancing enemy force, believers must not turn their backs, the clearest command not to leave one's opponent.
Those left behind rejoice in sitting, dislike striving, and invoke the heat; bodily difficulty becomes their reason for refusing the campaign.
A group falsely claims its houses are exposed while intending only flight, so false speech and battlefield desertion become one failure.
They had covenanted not to turn their backs, making staying in the fight a trust for which they will be questioned.
When fighting is prescribed, those with diseased hearts look toward the Prophet like one fainting at death, exposing collapse at the moment of the charge.
Once the matter is resolved, being true to God would be better for them; truth here means carrying through the battle duty feared in 47:20.
Believers are forbidden to weaken and call for peace while they have the upper hand and God will not deprive them of the fruit of their works.
The desert Arabs left behind offer family and property as excuses and say with their tongues what is not in their hearts; lagging and unreliable speech coincide.
Those left behind will be called to fight a formidable people; obedience brings a good reward, while turning away repeats the earlier failure.
Believers are challenged for saying what they do not do, locating falsity in an announced action that never reaches performance.
God intensely hates saying what one does not do, confirming that broken action rather than vocabulary alone is at issue in 61:2.
God loves fighters in a solid rank like a compact structure; their unmoving cohesion reverses the warrior who abandons his opponent.
Israel tells Moses to fight without them while they remain sitting, an explicit refusal to move from road to battle.
Their refusal produces forty years of wandering in the land, turning stationary disobedience in 5:24 into a journey that cannot reach its end.
Saul's army is tested on the road by the river; most drink, a small group crosses, and some declare they have no strength for the fight, sorting endurance from exhaustion.
Those who continue into battle ask for poured-out patience and firm feet, the sustaining answer to the weakness voiced in 2:249.
Those eager to campaign but lacking a mount to carry them turn away weeping; the ayah separates involuntary lack of transport from the moral faltering of the able.
The panting chargers stage the mount exerting itself at speed, directly opposing the horse that falls behind.
Their hooves strike sparks, contributing the physical force of the sustained charge begun in 100:1.
They raid at dawn, making the dictionary's warrior charge a Quranic scene rather than a detached lexical gloss.
They raise a cloud of dust in the charge, showing continued forward force after the initial rush.
They penetrate the center of the gathered force, carrying the charge to completion rather than slackening midway.
Moses declares that he will not cease until reaching the meeting of the seas even if he travels for ages, a direct vow not to stop on the road.
After passing the place, Moses names the fatigue met on the journey, نَصَبًا, giving the section an explicit Quranic scene of travel exhaustion.
One who leaves home emigrating toward God and is overtaken by death still has a secured reward, so even a journey physically cut short need not lose its wage.
Those who emigrate and are killed or die are promised a beautiful provision, another assurance that a severed road does not sever divine payment.
God shows the human the two elevated ways, establishing the difficult road on which endurance and choice are tested.
The human does not attempt the steep ascent, ٱلْعَقَبَةَ, an image of failing to press into the hard part of the road.
The successful climber belongs among believers who counsel patience and mercy, naming the endurance needed for the ascent of 90:11.
Those who strive for God are guided into His paths, سُبُلَنَا, joining sustained effort to a road disclosed by the destination.
The human has only what he strives for, placing recompense on the labor actually carried through.
That striving will be seen, so effort does not vanish unseen when the traveler tires.
The striving is then repaid with the fullest payment, completing the road from exertion to reward.
Whoever seeks the Hereafter and strives for it with the striving due to it while believing has an effort that is thanked, a positive pattern of work reaching its intended end.
The work of a believer who does righteous deeds will not be denied, and it is written down; this protects effort from the failure implied by interrupted payment.
The people of the Garden are told that their striving has been thanked, identifying lasting provision as the recognition of completed effort.
The ayah gathers measured night work, sickness, travelers seeking provision, and fighters, then orders what is manageable; divine knowledge adjusts exertion without erasing its reward.
The Quraysh are held together by accustomed security, the human social analogue of a mount trusted to keep the journey possible.
Their winter and summer caravan journeys make repeated, dependable travel the concrete content of the security named in 106:1.
They are commanded to worship the Lord of the House in response to the dependable journeys of 106:2.
Feeding against hunger and granting safety from fear supply the provision and security that keep those journeys from breaking down.
Visible towns are set at measured stages and travelers are told to journey by night and day in safety, ءَامِنِينَ, a fully provisioned road.
The people ask that the distances between stages be lengthened and are dispersed into tales, reversing the safe, measured journey of 34:18 into rupture.
A town secure and tranquil with abundant provision denies God's favors, so fear and hunger replace reliability; security, supply, and denial turn together.
Among livestock are animals made for carrying loads, حَمُولَةً, the direct Quranic class corresponding to the section's load camels.
Livestock provide drink from their bellies and many benefits, supplying the milk and usefulness expected from the section's working animals.
People are carried on livestock and ships, adding transport to the provision named in 23:21.
God creates pairs and makes ships and livestock for riding, grounding the mount's capacity in created fitness.
The rider settles on the animal's back and glorifies the One who subjected it because humans could not master it unaided.
The rider acknowledges the return to the Lord, making each mounted journey a figure for the final destination of human toil.
God makes livestock so that people ride some and eat from others, directly presenting the animal as a fitted mount.
Livestock meet needs in human breasts, and people are carried on them and on ships, widening the burden-bearer's service beyond a single trip.
Livestock are subjected so that some become mounts and others food, naming riding as one reason they are placed under human use.
Other benefits and drinks come from the same animals, linking transport to the expected provision that can continue or fail.
Horses, mules, and donkeys are created for riding and adornment, supplying the exact animal world behind the lagging horse and dependable mount.
Solomon is shown fine, swift steeds standing poised, a Quranic counterpart to the source dictionary's leading horses rather than the belated one.
His attachment to the good of the horses lasts until they disappear from sight, showing the attraction and possible diversion bound to these prized mounts.
He commands that the horses be returned, رُدُّوهَا, placing the section's return-root inside the scene of swift steeds.
Abraham asks that the place be made a secure town, بَلَدًا ءَامِنًا, joining the same two word families whose secondary senses become lagging horse and reliable camel in the section.
Abraham again asks that this town be secure, ٱلْبَلَدَ ءَامِنًا; the ordinary Quranic pairing clarifies the semantic ground from which the animal contrast is drawn.
Whoever enters the House is safe, and pilgrimage is owed by whoever can find a way to it; safety, road, and capacity to travel meet at the sanctuary.
On a journey without a scribe, a trusted person must discharge the trust placed in him, joining travel conditions to practical reliability.
The firmest handhold has no break, لَا ٱنفِصَامَ لَهَا; this unbreakable support is the exact counterimage to the dictionary's weak cord, المَنِين.
One who submits to God while doing good has grasped the firmest handhold, so faithful work is secured by the opposite of a weak rope.
The command to hold fast together to God's cord makes the cord a sustaining bond, illuminating by reversal the section's menīn cord that cannot be relied upon.
Those who say their Lord is God and then remain steadfast, ٱسْتَقَامُوا۟, turn the ق و م family into continued fidelity rather than an exhausted animal's stationary standing.
Those who confess God and remain steadfast have neither fear nor grief; istiqāmah is again standing that carries the journey through.
The Prophet and those who repent are commanded to remain straight as ordered, فَٱسْتَقِمْ, reversing the root's dictionary scene of stopping because movement has failed.
Remaining straight upon the way, ٱسْتَقَامُوا۟ عَلَى ٱلطَّرِيقَةِ, would bring abundant water; steadfast road and continuing provision directly oppose stoppage and depletion.
Hypocrites rise for prayer only lazily, قَامُوا۟ كُسَالَىٰ, a moral instance in which standing coincides with drained willingness rather than vigorous work.
The command to stand through the night turns قيام into demanding sustained service rather than immobility.
A weighty word is about to be cast upon the one commanded to stand in 73:2, explaining that this standing is endurance under a load.
كَلَّا بَلْ تُكَذِّبُونَ بِٱلدِّينِ is the closest direct parallel to the denial of Judgment questioned in 95:7.
The transgressors are defined as those who deny the Day of Judgment, again locating كذب at the final accounting toward which the traveler works.
The condemned confess that they used to deny the Day of Judgment, showing the endpoint of a denial that persisted until certainty arrived.
The person denies and turns away, كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, pairing false response with bodily withdrawal as the section pairs a false charge with faltering.
The question supposes one who denies and turns away, كَذَّبَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ, again making denial an action that retreats.
If the condemned were returned, رُدُّوا۟, they would return to what they were forbidden and are liars, لَكَٰذِبُونَ; two source roots meet in repeated moral failure.
God's messenger identifies God's she-camel and her drink; the literal she-camel prepares the act of denial in 91:14.
They deny the messenger and hamstring the she-camel, فَكَذَّبُوهُ فَعَقَرُوهَا, an unusually exact meeting of the section's camel world and its كذب root.
Thamud denies the warnings, introducing the camel trial that follows in 54:27.
God sends the she-camel as a test to the people who denied, so the animal itself becomes the measure of whether their response will prove true.
Water is apportioned between the people and the she-camel, making reliable provision and its measured turn part of the test.
They call their companion and he hamstrings the she-camel, completing the failure announced by denial in 54:23.
Thamud denies the messengers, opening another passage in which denial will be tested through a literal she-camel.
The she-camel has an allotted drink and the people an allotted drink on a known day, a measured provision endangered by their response.
They hamstring her and become regretful, completing in action the denial stated in 26:141.
The she-camel is presented as God's sign and must be left to feed on God's earth, a literal camel entrusted to the people's restraint.
They hamstring the she-camel and defy their Lord's command, turning the entrusted animal of 7:73 into evidence of their failed fidelity.
Salih presents God's she-camel as a sign and commands that she be left to feed, another camel-centered test of whether a charge will be honored.
They hamstring her and receive a three-day deadline, showing the trust in 11:64 broken by decisive action.
The command to look at how camels were created directs attention to the very creature whose capacities the section's dictionary senses unfold.
At the final upheaval even valuable pregnant she-camels are left untended; the animal normally relied upon for future milk and wealth loses its worldly function.
Livestock yield pure, pleasant milk from within their bodies, supplying the Quranic provision against which the dictionary's prematurely failing camel milk can be heard.
Joseph's brothers expect to add a camel-load of measure and call it easy, another Quranic use of the camel as the unit of carried provision.
Believers must prepare all possible force, including tethered war-horses, the material readiness that precedes a charge capable of being sustained.
Those fleeing the Reminder are likened to startled donkeys, turning an animal's flight into the image of an unreliable human response.
The donkeys flee from a lion, completing the flight scene of 74:50 and contrasting with the animal or warrior that holds its course.
Voluntary spending explicitly includes the stranded traveler, making generosity the communal means by which one halted on the road can continue.
Good treatment is commanded for the nearby companion and the stranded traveler, placing road vulnerability within ordinary human responsibility.
A share of spoils is assigned to the stranded traveler, turning the proceeds of battle into support for one whose journey has failed.
Obligatory charity includes the stranded traveler, a formal provision for the human counterpart of the road-stopped mount.
The traveler is to be given his due along with kin and the needy, answering interrupted movement with a concrete claim on resources.
Giving the traveler his due is called better for those seeking God's face, so aiding a broken journey becomes enduring work.
Communal revenue is directed in part to the stranded traveler so wealth does not circulate only among the rich, providing the road-bound person from a shared load.
The human is created anxiously unstable, a general disposition that explains why a bearer may fail under changing conditions.
When harm touches him he becomes impatient, naming the inward collapse corresponding to exhaustion on the road.
When good touches him he withholds it, joining the same instability to the section's secondary image of weakening even in generosity.
When called to spend, some are stingy, and turning away risks replacement by others; refusal to carry generosity through becomes loss of one's place.
Some people's striving goes astray in the nearer life while they think they are doing well, a path of labor whose apparent effort never reaches the true destination.
Death and life are created to test who is best in work, making human fitness for عمل accountable rather than merely productive.
Believing men and women who do good work receive a good life and a reward according to their best deeds, the fruitful outcome of sustained عمل.
Enduring good deeds are better in reward and in return, مَرَدًّا, joining what remains of work to the section's return-root.
Wealth and children are temporary adornment, while enduring good deeds are better in reward and hope, distinguishing the provision that passes from the work that remains.
God wills to lighten people's obligations because the human was created weak, explicitly balancing imposed work against creaturely exhaustion.
Believers are commanded to strive while being told that no constriction was placed on them in religion, a boundary between strenuous service and an impossible load.

The heart did not falsify what it saw, مَا كَذَبَ ٱلْفُؤَادُ; this may illuminate the source formula فَمَا كَذَبَ only by contrast of domains, since here fidelity belongs to perception rather than a warrior's charge.
